title: Infra SE recruiting screen - Jordan Smith
summary: Initial 30-minute phone screen for Infra SE role. Candidate has 5+ years infra + ML serving experience; strong on Kubernetes, experience with GPU fleets and CUDA kernels, limited direct experience with quantization but understands tradeoffs. Agreed next step: take-home micro-assignment + technical loop if results look good.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-05 14:00 UTC — duration ~36m
Attendees: Taylor (Redwood), Priya (HM), Samir (SE), Jordan (candidate), Maya (coord)

[00:00] Taylor: ok hey Jordan, thanks for joining, can you hear us alright?
[00:06] Jordan: yeah hi, thanks for having me, can hear you fine.
[00:10] Priya: hi Jordan, I'm Priya, hiring manager, quick intros, then we'll ask a few background Qs and a couple tech ones.
[00:18] Jordan: sounds good.
[00:20] Taylor: quick housekeeping — this is a phone screen primarily, we might cover past infra work, Kubernetes, GPU infra, inference runtimes. It's about 30 minutes. Any time constraints?
[00:29] Jordan: I'm good for 40, no prob.
[00:31] Samir: hey Jordan, I'm Samir, Senior infra eng, will jump in on the more technical bits.
[00:36] Jordan: great thanks.
[00:40] Taylor: ok first — tell us a little about your last two roles and what you've actually built for ML serving. Keep it high level.
[00:48] Jordan: sure — last role was at Orion AI, I was infra lead for model serving. We managed a mixed fleet of on-prem GPUs and cloud instances. I built the autoscaling controller for batch and realtime endpoints, worked on optimizing batching logic, and did a bunch of work around prefix KV caching for chat style workloads — we used a custom caching layer that sat in front of the inference nodes. Prior to that I was at Nebula Labs where I focused on Kubernetes ops, CI/CD, and packaging models into container images with fused libs for CUDA/rocm.
[01:20] Priya: ok nice. You're saying you implemented KV cache — was that a Redis-based approach or in-process?
[01:25] Jordan: so hybrid — we used Redis for persistent session state but had an in-memory LRU on the node for hot prefixes to reduce RTT. It was... there were tradeoffs — invalidation was tricky with replicas. Some mis-syncs early on.
[01:38] Samir: how did you handle KV cache consistency across autoscaled nodes — did you favor local cache with eventual consistency or a centralized cache?
[01:44] Jordan: local-first. We tuned TTLs and used a write-through to Redis on miss, so correctness was eventual. Latency wins for hot prefixes. We also co-located workers with the cache when possible to reduce network hops.
[01:56] Taylor: great, curious about GPU infra — which frameworks/stack are you most familiar with? TensorRT, ONNX, Triton?
[02:04] Jordan: familiar with Triton in prod, we used it for TensorFlow and PyTorch backends, also did TensorRT conversions for quantized models. Also custom kernels in CUDA for a small transformer variant where inference perf mattered. I wrote a couple CUDA kernels to speed up custom attention ops — not huge scale but helped.
[02:22] Priya: you mentioned quantization — what's your experience there? 8-bit? 4-bit? Post-training quant or QAT?
[02:29] Jordan: mostly PTQ 8-bit, we've started experimenting with mixed-precision and 4-bit quant using QAT for sensitive layers. I know the tradeoffs: some models drop accuracy on naive 4-bit, and re-training helps. We relied on eval suites to monitor WER/metric drift. Not a quantization researcher but hands-on.
[02:45] Samir: did you ever have to build fallbacks for degraded accuracy — like route to FP16 variant when quality dips?
[02:50] Jordan: yes we had a routing layer — traffic split by policy: high-priority customers to FP16 until the quantized model passed checks, or we did A/B test rollouts with shadow traffic.
[03:02] Taylor: nice, that maps well to our platform thinking. How about deployment models — have you deployed VPC/private setups or on-prem air-gapped infra?
[03:09] Jordan: yes both. At Orion we had a VPC private cluster in a colo, and also helped a finance customer with air-gapped setup — packaging images onto encrypted USB, local K8s with restricted egress, and KMS integration for model keys.
[03:24] Priya: security wise, what tooling did you use for key management and audit logs?
[03:28] Jordan: we integrated HashiCorp Vault for secrets and KMS for key wrapping, logs shipped to an internal ELK stack with restricted retention policies. SOC2 stuff mostly handled by our security team but I interfaced with them.
[03:38] Taylor: switching gears, can you walk me through a time you diagnosed a perf regression in inference latency? Steps you took.
[03:45] Jordan: sure — we had a regression after a library upgrade, p95 latency spiked. First I triaged with perf traces and flame graphs, saw a specific memcpy and kernel launch overhead that increased. Reproduced with a synthetic load, then rolled back the lib to confirm. For a long-term fix we optimized the kernel launch path and adjusted batching heuristics — reduced tail latency by ~20%.
[04:08] Samir: what profiling tools did you use? NVIDIA Nsight? perf?
[04:12] Jordan: Nsight compute/profiler, CUPTI traces, also eBPF for syscall level analysis on the host. For network stacks we used tc and iperf.
[04:21] Priya: what about model orchestration — are you familiar with model cataloging/versioning and rollouts?
[04:26] Jordan: yes, we used a model registry (custom) with metadata: model hash, quant profile, expected cost per token, and deployment spec. Rollouts via canary with canary % and automatic rollback on quality regression.
[04:37] Taylor: great. A few quick hypotheticals — if you had a tight latency SLO and cost pressure, how would you approach choosing between aggressive quantization and more powerful GPU instances?
[04:46] Jordan: I'd run a cost-latency-quality matrix: measure token/sec and accuracy for quantized variants and for bigger GPUs; if quantization gives similar quality with lower cost per token I'd prefer it, but if accuracy hit is unacceptable then bigger GPUs or batching tuning. Also explore caching hot prefixes to reduce compute.
[05:04] Samir: another one — we've got KV cache invalidation issues in a multi-replica autoscale world. Any concrete strategies?
[05:11] Jordan: yes — introduce a coherence layer: a light pub/sub (Kafka/Rabbit) for invalidation events, or use sticky routing to keep session affinity on same replica, or use a sharded centralized cache with low-latency links. Each has tradeoffs for complexity and tail latency.
[05:28] Priya: ok cool. Now some behavioural— how do you communicate perf tradeoffs to product/stakeholders who want lower latency but also lower cost?
[05:36] Jordan: I present concrete numbers and options: e.g., 30% lower latency via X would cost Y more per 1M tokens; show expected user impact and provide recommended fallback. Use dashboards and simple biz metrics so stakeholders can decide.
[05:49] Taylor: any red flags in your job history we should know?
[05:53] Jordan: no red flags — left last role for relocation reasons, and a restructure.
[05:58] Maya: quick scheduling note — if you pass this screen, we'll ask for a 60-min deep technical loop.
[06:03] Jordan: understood.
[06:06] Taylor: ok couple more quick specifics — experience with Triton scaling?
[06:09] Jordan: yes we used Triton for multi-model endpoints, used model control API to load/unload large models and tuned instance groups. Also set concurrency and preferred batch settings per model.
[06:21] Priya: any experience with operator-level optimizations — e.g., custom fused ops or attention kernels?
[06:26] Jordan: built a fused attention kernel in CUDA for a specialized transformer variant, that reduced memory copies by fusing softmax+matmul sequences. Not upstreamed, used internally.
[06:36] Samir: do you have experience working with multi-tenant isolation and throttling?
[06:40] Jordan: yes — token quotas, per-tenant rate limits, fair queueing in the routing layer; also resource pools per customer to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[06:50] Taylor: ok we'll wrap with culture fit — how do you like collaborating with research teams vs infra?
[06:55] Jordan: enjoy cross-functional work; prefer clear SLAs and experiments with guardrails. I like pairing with researchers to identify production constraints early.
[07:06] Priya: any compensation expectations or timing constraints?
[07:10] Jordan: target base 180-200k and open to equity. Timeline: interviewing now, can start in 4-6 weeks.
[07:19] Taylor: good to know. Anything you want to ask us?
[07:22] Jordan: yeah curious about Redwood infra scale — typical cluster sizes and cloud/on-prem split?
[07:27] Samir: currently mix: hosted API on cloud regions, dedicated pools for reserved customers, ranges from small dedicated clusters to multi-A100 pools. We also offer private deployments for enterprise.
[07:40] Jordan: that sounds like the work I'd expect — excited about the routing and batching pieces.
[07:44] Taylor: cool. We'll send the take-home micro assignment which covers a short design + small profiling exercise. If that looks good, we'll bring you in for the technical loop.
[07:53] Jordan: sounds great. Thanks for your time.
[07:56] Priya: thanks Jordan.
[07:58] Taylor: thanks — we'll follow up.
[08:00] [call ends and short background chatter, audio drops and a recorded voicemail beep]

Note: transcription contains minor errors where proper nouns or acronyms may be slightly off (e.g., "Triton" sometimes transcribed as "Triden"), and timestamps are approximate.
